title: Mechanical Ventilation: Lung‑Protective Settings and Evidence‑Based Weaning
summary: Prioritize low tidal volume ventilation with constraints on plateau and driving pressures, judicious PEEP titration, and early, protocolized liberation. Evidence from landmark trials and contemporary syntheses supports strategies that reduce ventilator‑induced lung injury and improve clinical outcomes in ARDS. Apply structured daily readiness assessments, spontaneous breathing trials, and sedation minimization to accelerate safe weaning.
clinicalQuestion: What lung‑protective ventilator settings and weaning protocols improve outcomes and minimize ventilator‑induced lung injury in adults with acute respiratory failure/ARDS?

keyMoments.title: Lung‑Protective Core
keyMoments.body: Use **low tidal volumes (~6 mL/kg PBW)** with **plateau ≤30 cm H2O** and **driving pressure minimization**; these strategies reduce VILI and improve outcomes in ARDS [2], [1].

keyMoments.title: Pressure Targets that Matter
keyMoments.body: **Driving pressure (ΔP = Pplat − PEEP)** correlates with mortality; reducing ΔP within lung‑protective ventilation is associated with better survival signals [2].

keyMoments.title: Readiness and SBTs
keyMoments.body: Daily **weaning readiness checks** followed by **spontaneous breathing trials (SBT)** using low‑support methods shorten ventilation duration and complications when paired with sedation‑light strategies [3].

keyMoments.title: Personalization and Monitoring
keyMoments.body: When available, consider **recruitability assessment** to individualize PEEP; avoid injurious overdistension or derecruitment [1].

keyMoments.title: Early Application Beyond ICU
keyMoments.body: Initiating **lung‑protective settings in the ED** lowers pulmonary complications downstream, supporting early protocolization [3].

sections.title: Lung‑Protective Ventilation: Practical Implementation
sections.blurb: Align settings to minimize mechanical stress and strain while meeting gas exchange goals. Emphasize low VT, pressure limits, and cautious PEEP titration.

steps.title: Set Mode and Tidal Volume
steps.body: Choose volume‑assist control (or pressure‑targeted equivalent ensuring consistent low VT). Target **~6 mL/kg PBW (allow 4–8)**; adjust based on compliance and PaCO2/pH, tolerating permissive hypercapnia if pH ≥7.20 [1].

steps.title: Limit Pressures
steps.body: Measure plateau pressure with an inspiratory hold; keep **Pplat ≤30 cm H2O**. Track **driving pressure (ΔP)** and aim to keep **ΔP ≤14–15 cm H2O** by lowering VT or optimizing PEEP when safe [2], [1].

steps.title: PEEP and FiO2
steps.body: Use ARDS‑style PEEP/FiO2 tables as a starting point; escalate PEEP judiciously to improve oxygenation while avoiding overdistension. Target **SpO2 88–95%** and minimize FiO2 as soon as feasible [3], [1].

steps.title: Recruitment and Personalization
steps.body: Avoid routine aggressive recruitment maneuvers. Consider **recruitability‑guided** approaches (e.g., R/I ratio, imaging/EIT) to tailor PEEP in selected patients; evidence favors selective rather than universal recruitment [1].

steps.title: Synchrony and Sedation
steps.body: Use light sedation and address patient–ventilator asynchrony with trigger/cycle adjustments or short courses of neuromuscular blockade if severe; minimize exposure to avoid delayed weaning [1].

sections.title: Weaning Readiness and Spontaneous Breathing Trials
sections.blurb: Protocolized assessments shorten ventilation and reduce complications when paired with sedation minimization and early oxygen weaning.

cards.title: Readiness to Wean: Daily Screen
items: Hemodynamic stability (no escalating vasopressors)
Improving or stable gas exchange: SpO2 ≥88–90% on FiO2 ≤0.40–0.50 and PEEP ≤8 cm H2O
Adequate mental status and cough; manageable secretions
No active procedures or immediate need for deep sedation
Low ventilator demands: RR <35, VT adequate, acceptable pH

cards.title: SBT Methods
items: T‑piece or minimal support (PS 0–5 cm H2O, PEEP 0–5) for 30–120 minutes
Pass if: RR <35, SpO2 ≥88–90%, HR and BP stable, no distress, pH acceptable
If fail: identify reversible causes (fluid overload, bronchospasm, excessive sedation), treat, retry in 24 hours

cards.title: Sedation Strategy
items: Daily sedation interruption or light‑sedation targets
Analgesia‑first approach; avoid benzodiazepines when possible
Assess delirium and address reversible factors

cards.title: Post‑SBT Extubation Readiness
items: Airway protection: strong cough, manageable secretions
Cuff‑leak test in high‑risk laryngeal edema
Plan for post‑extubation support (HFNC/NIV) in high‑risk patients

cards.title: Safety and VILI Prevention
items: Avoid VT creep: re‑confirm PBW and set hard VT alarms
Reassess Pplat and ΔP after any setting change
Early FiO2 weaning to limit oxygen toxicity [3]

cards.title: When to Re‑Evaluate Strategy
items: Pplat >30 or ΔP rising despite low VT
Worsening oxygenation despite higher PEEP
Marked asynchrony or dynamic hyperinflation

sections.title: What the Literature Supports
sections.blurb: Synthesis of high‑value findings to guide bedside decisions.

cards.title: Low VT and Pressure Limits
items: The ARDS low‑VT strategy is foundational: **~6 mL/kg PBW, Pplat ≤30 cm H2O**; consistently reduces VILI and improves survival signals in ARDS [1].

cards.title: Driving Pressure Matters
items: Across trials of lung‑protective ventilation, **lower ΔP** is associated with improved survival; aim to minimize ΔP by adjusting VT/PEEP within safe limits [2].

cards.title: Early, Protocolized Care
items: ED‑initiated lung‑protective bundles (low VT, appropriate PEEP, rapid FiO2 weaning) reduce pulmonary complications after ICU admission [3].

cards.title: Personalized PEEP and Recruitment
items: Use recruitability assessment to avoid injurious overdistension; evidence favors **selective** recruitment over routine maneuvers [1].

cards.title: Mechanical Power and VILI
items: High mechanical power components (VT, RR, pressures, flow) contribute to VILI; strategies that reduce power may mitigate injury, though implementation challenges remain [4], [5].
